pos: n. (the part of a plant that fixes and feeds it; figuratively, origin and source; rendering Hebrew shoresh, Greek rhiza)
etymology: From Old Norse rot, cognate with the Latin radix. In Scripture the root is always the hidden and determining part — what feeds the visible tree and what an axe is laid to when the tree is to be ended.
biblical_def: A root in Scripture is the hidden source that determines the visible thing, and it is used most strikingly of Christ. Isaiah prophesies from a felled dynasty: “there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isaiah 11:1) — a stem is what is left when a tree has been cut down, and the Messiah comes not from the standing house of David but from its stump. The servant song develops it: “he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness” (Isaiah 53:2). Nothing about the soil or the shoot promised anything. Revelation then reverses the genealogy in a single clause: “I am the root and the offspring of David” (Revelation 22:16) — he is David's descendant according to the flesh and David's source according to his deity, which is exactly the puzzle he put to the Pharisees about how David could call his son Lord. Paul uses the word for a moral origin: “the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows” (1 Timothy 6:10). The verse is commonly misquoted as though money were the root; the text says the love of it, and names two consequences — erring from the faith, and self-inflicted grief.
webster_summary: The hidden part that fixes and feeds. Messiah comes as a shoot from a felled stump and a root out of dry ground, and calls himself both the root and the offspring of David; the love of money is named the root of all evil.
webster_full: ROOT, n. [Sw. rot; L. radix.] That part of a plant which enters and fixes itself in the earth, and serves to support the plant in an erect position.
2. The part of any thing that resembles the roots of a plant in manner of growth.
3. The origin or cause of any thing; that from which a thing proceeds; as, the love of money is the root of all evil.
4. The bottom or lower part of any thing; as the root of a mountain.
5. A race; a family; descendants; as, the root of Jesse, Is. 11.
corruption_summary: 1 Timothy 6:10 is misquoted to condemn money itself, which lets the actual sin escape — and the root is treated as the visible symptom rather than the hidden appetite Paul names.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular form of the verse — money is the root of all evil — is not what Paul wrote, and the difference matters in both directions. It lets a poor man think himself safe when covetousness is fully available to those who have nothing, and it lets a rich man think himself condemned when Scripture nowhere forbids wealth as such: Abraham was rich, Job was restored to more than he had, and Paul in the same chapter instructs the rich rather than dismissing them, charging them to trust in the living God rather than in uncertain riches and to be rich in good works. The condemned thing is the love, an appetite that operates equally at every income, and its symptoms are erring from the faith and piercing oneself through with many sorrows — both self-administered.

The principle to recover is Isaiah's stump. The house of David was cut down; the throne was empty and the family reduced to a carpenter in a village. From that stem comes the rod, and from those roots the Branch, so that the very hopelessness of the wood is part of the sign. Isaiah 53 says the same of the man — a root out of a dry ground, with no form or comeliness that anyone should desire him. God's way of bringing his greatest work out of what looks finished and unpromising is not an occasional exception in Scripture; it is his settled manner, and it should govern how a Christian reads the state of his own soil.
roots_summary: Hebrew shoresh is a root, and by extension a bottom or origin; geza is the stem or stump of a felled tree. Greek rhiza is a root, used of Christ and of the love of money.
roots_lines: Hebrew shoresh (H8328) — a root; also the origin or lowest part of a thing.
Hebrew geza (H1503) — a stock or stump of a felled tree; the stem of Jesse, Isaiah 11:1.
Hebrew netser (H5342) — a shoot, a branch; the rod that comes out of the stem.
Greek rhiza (G4491) — a root; the root of David, and the root of all evil.
Greek philarguria (G5365) — love of money, avarice; the actual root named in 1 Timothy 6:10.
usage: Of Messiah from a felled house: a Branch shall grow out of his roots (Isaiah 11:1).
Of the unpromising soil: as a root out of a dry ground (Isaiah 53:2).
Of the hidden moral origin: the love of money is the root of all evil (1 Timothy 6:10).

And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots:
Isaiah 53:2
For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him.
1 Timothy 6:10

Revelation 22:16
I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star.

pos: n. (one sent with a message; rendering Hebrew malak, Greek angelos)
etymology: From Old French messagier, from Latin missus, sent. Hebrew malak and Greek angelos both mean simply one sent, and the same word serves for a human courier and for an angel — the office is defined by the sending, not by the nature of the one sent.
biblical_def: A messenger in Scripture is defined entirely by who sent him and what he carries. Malachi contains the greatest instance, and it names two: “Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant” (Malachi 3:1). The first messenger is John the Baptist, and Mark opens his Gospel by quoting it: “Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee” (Mark 1:2). But notice the grammar of Malachi's promise — the messenger prepares the way before me, and the one who then comes is the Lord. The verse assumes the deity of the coming one, which is why the New Testament applies it to Christ without argument. Haggai bears the plain title in a short and remarkable verse: “Then spake Haggai the LORD'S messenger in the LORD'S message unto the people, saying, I am with you, saith the LORD” (Haggai 1:13). The whole sermon is four words long. And Isaiah shows a messenger who has failed at the one thing required: “Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent?” (Isaiah 42:19) — a courier who cannot see or hear is not a messenger but an ornament.
webster_summary: One sent with a message; the same word serves for a courier and an angel. Malachi's messenger prepares the way before the LORD himself; Haggai preaches four words; Isaiah exposes a messenger who cannot hear.
webster_full: MESSENGER, n. [Fr. messager.] One who bears a message or an errand; the bearer of a verbal or written communication.
2. One who conveys dispatches from one prince or court to another; a courier.
3. A harbinger; a forerunner; he or that which foreshows.
4. MESSAGE, n. Any notice, word or communication, written or verbal, sent from one person to another.
5. In Scripture, an angel, or one sent of God; I send my messenger before thy face, Mal. 3.
corruption_summary: The messenger is honoured or judged for himself rather than for his message, so that the office is made a platform — and the plainness of a true message is mistaken for a lack of substance.
corruption_paragraphs: The whole authority of a messenger is borrowed. He has none of his own, may add nothing, and is answerable for delivering exactly what he was given. This is why John the Baptist's self-description is the model — a voice, not a personality; and why he could say He must increase, but I must decrease without any sense of loss. Where preaching becomes a platform, the messenger's own qualities become the message, and the congregation ends up evaluating a man rather than hearing God. Isaiah's rebuke names the occupational disease exactly: a messenger who is deaf. A man who has stopped listening cannot carry anything but himself.

The principle to recover is the sufficiency of Haggai 1:13. The messenger of the LORD, in the LORD's message, said this to a discouraged people who had left God's house in ruins: I am with you, saith the LORD. That is the whole sermon, and the next verse records that the LORD stirred up the spirit of the governor, of the high priest, and of all the remnant of the people, and they came and did work. Four words moved a nation to build. It is a standing rebuke to the assumption that a message must be elaborate to be powerful, and a standing comfort to any messenger who fears he has too little to say.
roots_summary: Hebrew malak is one sent — a human messenger or an angel; the noun malakuth is the message itself. Greek angelos is likewise a messenger, and gives the English angel.
roots_lines: Hebrew malak (H4397) — a messenger, one sent; used of prophets, couriers, and angels alike.
Hebrew malakuth (H4400) — a message; in the LORD'S message, Haggai 1:13.
Hebrew tsir (H6735) — an envoy, an ambassador; a faithful messenger is health, Proverbs 13:17.
Greek angelos (G32) — a messenger, an angel; the word of Malachi 3:1 in the Septuagint and Mark 1:2.
Greek apostolos (G652) — one sent forth, an apostle; the same idea raised to an office.
usage: Of the forerunner promised: I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me (Malachi 3:1).
Of a four-word sermon: Haggai the LORD'S messenger… I am with you, saith the LORD (Haggai 1:13).
Of a messenger who cannot hear: or deaf, as my messenger that I sent? (Isaiah 42:19).
scriptures: Malachi 3:1

Behold, I will send my messenger, and he shall prepare the way before me: and the Lord, whom ye seek, shall suddenly come to his temple, even the messenger of the covenant, whom ye delight in: behold, he shall come, saith the LORD of hosts.
Mark 1:2
As it is written in the prophets, Behold, I send my messenger before thy face, which shall prepare thy way before thee.
Haggai 1:13
Then spake Haggai the LORD'S messenger in the LORD'S message unto the people, saying, I am with you, saith the LORD.
Isaiah 42:19
Who is blind, but my servant? or deaf, as my messenger that I sent? who is blind as he that is perfect, and blind as the LORD'S servant?

pos: n. and v. (tender feeling for another's suffering, moving to help; rendering Hebrew chamal and chus, Greek eleeo)
etymology: From Old French pite, from the Latin pietas, dutiful affection — the same root as piety. The two English words parted company, but the shared origin is telling: pity in its old sense was a duty owed, not merely a feeling had.
biblical_def: Pity in Scripture is feeling that acts, and its finest statement is a father's: “Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him” (Psalm 103:13). The verse is bounded on both sides — the next verse gives the reason, for he knoweth our frame; he remembereth that we are dust — so God's pity is grounded in an accurate assessment of what we are, not in an indulgent one. It is promised to a nation: “Then will the LORD be jealous for his land, and pity his people” (Joel 2:18), coming immediately after the call to rend the heart and not the garments. Its absence is the mark of abandonment. Ezekiel describes Jerusalem's origin as an exposed newborn: “None eye pitied thee, to do any of these unto thee, to have compassion upon thee; but thou wast cast out in the open field” (Ezekiel 16:5) — and the chapter goes on to say that God passed by, saw her in her blood, and said unto her, Live. And Job asks his friends for it in the most desolate terms in the book: “Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me” (Job 19:21). He repeats the plea because the first time did not reach them. Six chapters later he is still being answered with theology instead.
webster_summary: Tender feeling that acts. The LORD pities as a father, knowing our frame; his pity is promised to a repenting people; and Job, receiving argument instead of it, must ask his friends twice.
webster_full: PITY, n. [Fr. pitie; L. pietas.] The feeling or suffering of one person, excited by the distresses of another; sympathy with grief or misery.
2. The ground or subject of pity; cause of grief; thing to be regretted.
3. PITY, v.t. To feel pain or grief for one in distress; to compassionate; to have sympathy for.
4. PITY, v.i. To be compassionate; to exercise pity.
5. In Scripture, like as a father pitieth his children, so the Lord pitieth them that fear him, Ps. 103.
corruption_summary: Pity is dismissed as condescension and replaced with abstract concern — while Job's friends show the older failure, answering a suffering man's plea for pity with correct doctrine.
corruption_paragraphs: Two failures surround this word. The modern one holds that pity is demeaning — that it looks down on its object — and prefers solidarity, awareness, or advocacy, none of which require being present with anyone. Scripture is unembarrassed by pity because God is said to have it, and no one accuses him of condescension who has understood Psalm 103:14: he pities because he knows our frame. Accurate knowledge of another's weakness, joined to tenderness rather than contempt, is not a lower thing than respect; it is what love looks like toward the fragile. The older failure is Job's friends, and it is the more dangerous in a doctrinally serious church. They sat with him seven days in silence and did well; then they spoke, and what they offered was a theology of suffering that was tidy, largely orthodox in its individual sentences, and entirely wrong about him. Job asked twice for pity and received arguments. God's verdict at the end is against them: ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath.

The principle to recover is what pity does in Ezekiel 16. No eye pitied the abandoned child; God passed by and saw her polluted in her own blood and said Live. Then he washed her, clothed her, and entered into covenant with her. The chapter is unsparing about what she became afterwards, and it is still where the doctrine of grace toward the helpless is stated most vividly in the prophets. Christian pity is patterned on that: it goes to the field, it does not wait to be asked twice, and it does something.
roots_summary: Hebrew chamal is to spare or pity; chus is to have compassion, literally of the eye that flows; racham is the womb-love of a parent. Greek eleeo is to show mercy.
roots_lines: Hebrew racham (H7355) — to love deeply, to pity; from rechem, the womb.
Hebrew chamal (H2550) — to spare, to have pity; the verb of Joel 2:18.
Hebrew chus (H2347) — to pity; literally that the eye should flow with compassion.
Hebrew yetser (H3336) — frame, form; he knoweth our frame, the ground of his pity.
Greek eleeo (G1653) — to have mercy, to pity; the cry of the blind men to the Son of David.
usage: Of the fatherly pity of God: like as a father pitieth his children (Psalm 103:13).
Of pity promised a repenting people: then will the LORD be jealous for his land, and pity his people (Joel 2:18).
Of a sufferer asking twice: have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends (Job 19:21).
scriptures: Psalm 103:13
Like as a father pitieth his children, so the LORD pitieth them that fear him.
Joel 2:18
Then will the LORD be jealous for his land, and pity his people.
Ezekiel 16:5
None eye pitied thee, to do any of these unto thee, to have compassion upon thee; but thou wast cast out in the open field, to the lothing of thy person, in the day that thou wast born.
Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me.

pos: n. (that which is eaten for nourishment; rendering Hebrew oklah and lechem, Greek trophe and diatrophe)
etymology: From the Saxon foda, akin to feed and to the Latin pasco, to feed. Hebrew lechem means bread and, by extension, food generally — the staple standing for the whole.
biblical_def: Food enters the Bible's story at the point where it becomes a temptation: “when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat” (Genesis 3:6). Three appetites are named — the body, the eye, and the mind — and John lists the same three as the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life. The fall came through something genuinely good for food, which is why asceticism has never been the biblical answer. Scripture is emphatic that God is the feeder: “Who giveth food to all flesh: for his mercy endureth for ever” (Psalm 136:25) — all flesh, believing or not, fed by mercy. Agur's prayer is the wisest thing in Scripture about how much a man should want: “give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with food convenient for me” (Proverbs 30:8), and he states the reason himself: “Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain” (Proverbs 30:9). And Job states the priority in a single line from the depth of his suffering: “I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food” (Job 23:12) — not more than luxury, but more than what he needed to live.
webster_summary: What is eaten for nourishment. The fall came through fruit good for food; God gives food to all flesh in mercy; Agur asks for neither poverty nor riches; and Job values God's words above his necessary food.
webster_full: FOOD, n. [Sax. foda.] In a general sense, whatever is eaten by animals for nourishment, and whatever supplies nutriment.
2. Meat; aliment; flesh or vegetables eaten for sustaining human life; victuals; provisions.
3. Whatever supplies nourishment and growth to plants.
4. Something that sustains, nourishes and augments; as, flattery is the food of vanity.
5. In Scripture, food convenient for me, Prov. 30; having food and raiment, let us be therewith content, 1 Tim. 6.
corruption_summary: Food is made either a moral system — purity by diet — or a matter of no consequence at all, when Scripture receives it with thanksgiving and treats appetite as a real spiritual front.
corruption_paragraphs: Paul warned Timothy that in the latter times some would depart from the faith, and the marks he named include commanding to abstain from meats which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth (1 Timothy 4:3-4). Diet as a road to holiness is an ancient error in permanent rotation, and its Christian versions still appear. Nothing God made is to be refused as unclean if it is received with thanksgiving; our Lord settled the question when he purged all meats. The opposite error treats appetite as spiritually irrelevant, though Scripture repeatedly makes the belly a rival god and lists gluttony and drunkenness together among the marks of a rebellious son.

The principle to recover is Agur's prayer, which almost nobody prays. He asks for neither poverty nor riches but for food convenient for me, and he gives the reason: full, he might deny God and say Who is the LORD?; poor, he might steal and take the name of his God in vain. Both extremes are named as spiritual dangers, which means prosperity is a risk to be prayed about and not only a blessing to be sought. Our Lord taught his disciples to ask for bread this day and daily, which is the same request in the same spirit — enough, and no stockpile that makes the asking unnecessary.
roots_summary: Hebrew lechem is bread and, by extension, food; oklah is that which is eaten. Greek trophe is nourishment; broma, meat or food.
roots_lines: Hebrew lechem (H3899) — bread, and food generally; the staple standing for the whole.
Hebrew oklah (H402) — food, that which is eaten; from akal, to eat.
Hebrew choq (H2706) — an appointed portion; the word behind food convenient for me.
Greek trophe (G5160) — nourishment, food; the labourer is worthy of his food, Matthew 10:10.
Greek broma (G1033) — meat, food; meats which God created to be received with thanksgiving.

Of God feeding all flesh: who giveth food to all flesh: for his mercy endureth for ever (Psalm 136:25).
Of the word valued above necessity: I have esteemed the words of his mouth more than my necessary food (Job 23:12).

And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.
Psalm 136:25
Who giveth food to all flesh: for his mercy endureth for ever.
Proverbs 30:9
Lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? or lest I be poor, and steal, and take the name of my God in vain.

pos: n. pl. (the fruit of the vine; rendering Hebrew anab, Greek staphule)
etymology: From Old French grape, a bunch or cluster, originally a hook used in harvesting. The English word names the cluster before the single berry, which is how Scripture almost always speaks of them — a cluster carried, gathered, or trodden.
biblical_def: Grapes in Scripture are the fruit by which a vine is judged. The spies bring back the evidence of Canaan: “they came unto the brook of Eshcol, and cut down from thence a branch with one cluster of grapes, and they bare it between two upon a staff” (Numbers 13:23) — a cluster requiring two men and a pole, and ten of the twelve who carried it still counselled against going in. Isaiah's song of the vineyard makes grapes the test of a nation: God fenced it, cleared the stones, planted the choicest vine, built a tower and a winepress, “and he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes” (Isaiah 5:2). Everything that could be done had been done; what failed was the fruit, and the chapter names it — he looked for judgment and beheld oppression, for righteousness and beheld a cry. Our Lord uses the same test for teachers: “Ye shall know them by their fruits. Do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles?” (Matthew 7:16) — the question expects the obvious answer, and Luke gives the same rule from the other side: “every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes” (Luke 6:44). It is the practical test for detecting false prophets. And Revelation uses the harvest for the last judgment: “gather the clusters of the vine of the earth; for her grapes are fully ripe” (Revelation 14:18). Ripeness is the signal, and the gathering is into the winepress of the wrath of God.
webster_summary: The fruit by which a vine is judged. Eshcol's cluster took two men to carry; Isaiah's vineyard had every advantage and yielded wild grapes; Christ makes fruit the test of teachers; Revelation harvests when the grapes are ripe.
webster_full: GRAPE, n. [Fr. grappe, a cluster or bunch.] The fruit of the vine, growing in clusters.
2. Grapes are of various colors, and are used for food, and for making wine.
3. A mangy tumor on the legs of a horse.
4. Grape-shot, a cluster of small iron balls confined in a canvas bag.
5. In Scripture, the gleaning of the grapes of Ephraim, Judg. 8; sour grapes, Ezek. 18.
corruption_summary: Teachers are assessed by gifting, popularity, or sincerity rather than by fruit — and Isaiah 5 is read as a general lament instead of the specific charge of injustice it makes.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 7:16 supplies the church's standing test for teachers, and it is regularly set aside for easier ones. Sincerity is not a fruit — a man may be entirely sincere and be a thornbush. Nor is a crowd a fruit, nor eloquence, nor even orthodoxy recited without a life to match. What our Lord means by fruit is filled out elsewhere: the fruit of the Spirit in a man's character, and the fruit of his doctrine in those who follow him. He puts this test immediately after warning of wolves in sheep's clothing, so the whole point is that appearance and profession will not distinguish them. It takes time to see fruit, which is why 1 Timothy 3 requires a man to be proved and not a novice.

The principle to recover is what Isaiah's vineyard was actually charged with. God had given it everything — a fenced hill, cleared stones, the choicest vine, a tower, a winepress — and looked for grapes. The wild grapes are named in verse 7 and they are not doctrinal errors: he looked for judgment, but behold oppression; for righteousness, but behold a cry. The woes that follow fall on those who join house to house and field to field, on those who call evil good and good evil, and on those who justify the wicked for reward. A church with every advantage that produces no justice has produced wild grapes, whatever its confession says.
roots_summary: Hebrew anab is a grape or cluster; beushim are wild or worthless grapes; eshkol is a cluster, and the name of the valley. Greek staphule is a bunch of grapes.

Hebrew beushim (H891) — wild, stinking, worthless grapes; what the vineyard yielded.
Hebrew eshkol (H811) — a cluster; also the name of the brook the spies came to.
Greek staphule (G4718) — a bunch of grapes; do men gather grapes of thorns?
Greek karpos (G2590) — fruit; the test by which teachers are known.
usage: Of the cluster carried between two: a branch with one cluster of grapes (Numbers 13:23).
Of a vineyard that failed its owner: he looked that it should bring forth grapes, and it brought forth wild grapes (Isaiah 5:2).
Of the test of teachers: do men gather grapes of thorns, or figs of thistles? (Matthew 7:16).

Isaiah 5:2

pos: a. (permitted by law; allowable; rendering Greek exesti, it is permitted)
etymology: From law, Saxon lagu, and the suffix -ful. The Greek behind most New Testament uses is the impersonal exesti, it is lawful or it is permitted — a word about permission rather than about obligation.
biblical_def: Lawful asks what is permitted, and Scripture repeatedly shows that it is not the last question. The Pharisees make it their first: “Behold, thy disciples do that which is not lawful to do upon the sabbath day” (Matthew 12:2), of men plucking ears of corn as they walked. Our Lord answers with David eating the shewbread and priests profaning the sabbath blamelessly, and then puts his own question, which reframes the whole category: “Is it lawful to do good on the sabbath days, or to do evil? to save life, or to kill?” (Mark 3:4) — and the text notes that they held their peace, because the question could not be answered without abandoning their position. Paul takes up the word twice with the same qualification: “All things are lawful unto me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but I will not be brought under the power of any” (1 Corinthians 6:12). He grants the liberty and then names two limits — usefulness, and mastery. A thing may be permitted and still unwise, and it may be permitted and still enslaving. Paul also uses the word to claim a civil right: “Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?” (Acts 22:25), which shows a Christian may lawfully appeal to law.
webster_summary: What is permitted — and never the last question. Christ asks whether it is lawful to do good on the sabbath; Paul grants that all things are lawful and adds two limits, expediency and mastery.
webster_full: LAWFUL, a. Agreeable to law; conformable to law; allowed by law; legal; legitimate.
2. Constituted by law; rightful; as the lawful owner of lands.
3. LAWFULLY, adv. Legally; in accordance with law.
4. LAWFULNESS, n. The quality of being conformable to law; legality.
5. In Scripture, permitted; it is not lawful for thee to have her, Matt. 14; all things are lawful for me, 1 Cor. 6.
corruption_summary: Christian liberty is treated as a verdict rather than a starting point — if a thing is lawful, no further question is asked — while the legalist asks only whether it is permitted and never whether it is good.
corruption_paragraphs: Two opposite parties both stop at the word lawful. The legalist asks what is permitted in order to draw a boundary and police it, and Matthew 12 shows where that ends: men able to identify a technical sabbath violation in hungry disciples, and unable to answer whether it is lawful to do good on the sabbath. Legalism is not an excess of seriousness about God's law; it is a substitution of a manageable rule for the law's actual intent. The antinomian asks the same question for the opposite reason — to establish that nothing forbids him — and treats a clean legal verdict as the end of the matter. Paul answers this second party directly, and it is worth noticing that he does not dispute the premise. He concedes all things are lawful and then says the concession settles less than they think.

The principle to recover is Paul's pair of tests. First, expediency: is this profitable, does it build up, does it serve anyone. Second, and sharper, mastery: I will not be brought under the power of any. A lawful thing that has begun to own a man has already answered the question, whatever the verdict on its lawfulness. This is a far more searching standard than a list of prohibitions, and it cannot be applied to a neighbour — only to oneself. Romans 14 adds the third consideration, the weaker brother, and between them these three settle nearly every question of Christian liberty without needing a new rule.
roots_summary: Greek exesti is the impersonal it is lawful, it is permitted. Hebrew has no exact equivalent; the Old Testament asks rather what is commanded or forbidden, which is itself instructive.

Hebrew mishpat (H4941) — judgment, ordinance, what is right; the Old Testament's framing of the question.

pos: a. and adv. (happening every day; of each day; rendering Hebrew tamid, continual, Greek epiousios and kath hemeran)
etymology: From day, Saxon daeg. Hebrew tamid means continual and is the term for the standing morning-and-evening sacrifice; the Greek epiousios in the Lord's prayer is nearly unique to that petition and probably means for the coming day.
biblical_def: Daily is Scripture's answer to the question of how often, and its repetitions are deliberate. The Lord's prayer contains the simplest: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Matthew 6:11) — both this day and daily, a request for today's supply that must be made again tomorrow, which is exactly how the manna was given and exactly why it was given that way. Discipleship is put on the same footing: “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross daily, and follow me” (Luke 9:23). Luke adds the word daily to a saying the other Gospels give without it, and it changes the picture from a single dramatic surrender to a repeated ordinary one. The Bereans are commended for a daily habit: they “received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so” (Acts 17:11) — and note that the searching was to test an apostle's preaching, which Luke calls more noble rather than presumptuous. And the first church kept the same rhythm: “continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart” (Acts 2:46).
webster_summary: Every day. Bread is asked for daily as the manna was given; the cross is taken up daily; the Bereans searched the scriptures daily; and the first church continued daily with one accord.
webster_full: DAILY, a. [Sax. daeglic, from daeg, day.] Happening or being every day; done day by day; bestowed or enjoyed every day; as daily labor; a daily allowance.
2. DAILY, adv. Every day; day by day; as, a thing happens daily.
3. Daily bread, the food necessary for each day, Matt. 6.
4. In Scripture, the daily sacrifice, the continual burnt offering of morning and evening, Num. 28.
5. DAY, n. That part of time in which the sun is above the horizon; also, the whole time or period of one revolution of the earth.
corruption_summary: The Christian life is imagined as a series of decisive moments rather than a daily rule, so that intensity replaces regularity — and Luke's daily is quietly dropped from taking up the cross.
corruption_paragraphs: Much popular Christianity is organised around events: a conference, a crisis, a rededication. Scripture's vocabulary is stubbornly repetitive. The sacrifice was tamid, continual, morning and evening for centuries. The manna fell every morning and bred worms if hoarded. The bread is asked for daily. The cross, in Luke's account, is taken up daily. God's ordinary way of forming a saint is not by rare intensity but by rhythms — which is also why the sabbath is weekly and the Supper is repeated. A man who has resolved something profound once and reads nothing on Tuesday has misunderstood the shape of the Christian life.

The principle to recover is the Bereans' habit and what it implies. They heard Paul — an apostle, preaching under inspiration — and then went home and searched the scriptures daily to see whether it was so, and the Holy Ghost calls them more noble for it. That settles two things at once. Scripture is the standard by which all preaching is measured, including the best; and a congregation that checks its pastor against the text is doing something commendable rather than disloyal. It also assumes a people who read enough, and often enough, to be able to check anything at all.
roots_summary: Hebrew tamid means continual, the standing morning-and-evening sacrifice; yom yom is day by day. Greek epiousios is the rare word of the Lord's prayer; kath hemeran is day by day.
roots_lines: Hebrew tamid (H8548) — continual, perpetual; the daily sacrifice of Exodus 29 and Numbers 28.
Hebrew yom (H3117) — a day; doubled, yom yom, meaning day by day.
Greek epiousios (G1967) — for the coming day, needful; the word rendered daily in Matthew 6:11.
Greek kath hemeran — day by day, daily; Luke's phrase for taking up the cross.
Greek kathemerinos (G2522) — daily; the daily ministration neglected in Acts 6:1.
usage: Of bread asked for one day at a time: give us this day our daily bread (Matthew 6:11).
Of the cross taken up repeatedly: take up his cross daily, and follow me (Luke 9:23).

pos: n. (elevation; distance upward; rendering Hebrew qomah and gobah, Greek hupsoma)
etymology: From the Saxon hehthu, from heah, high. Hebrew qomah is stature — the height of a man or a building; gobah carries the moral sense of loftiness and so of pride.
biblical_def: Height in Scripture measures buildings, men, and the reach of things that cannot separate us from God. It is plainly architectural in the ark's specification: “The length of the ark shall be three hundred cubits, the breadth of it fifty cubits, and the height of it thirty cubits” (Genesis 6:15) — exact dimensions given for a vessel no one had a use for yet. It measures a man, and is expressly dismissed as a criterion: of Eliab the LORD says, “Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the LORD seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7). Samuel, a prophet, had just been about to anoint the wrong man on the evidence of his build. Isaiah offers Ahaz a sign of any size he likes: “ask it either in the depth, or in the height above” (Isaiah 7:11) — and Ahaz refuses under a pretence of piety, so God gives the sign anyway, the virgin conceiving and bearing a son. And Paul closes his greatest chapter by putting height in a list of defeated things: “Nor height, nor depth, nor any other creature, shall be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 8:39).
webster_summary: Distance upward. It specifies the ark, and is expressly refused as a measure of a man — the LORD looketh on the heart — and stands last in Paul's list of things that cannot separate us from God's love.
webster_full: HEIGHT, n. hite. [Sax. hehthu, from heah, high.] Elevation above the ground; any indefinite distance above the earth.
2. The altitude of an object; the distance which any thing rises above its foot or basis.
3. Elevation of a star or other celestial object above the horizon.
4. Degree of latitude, either north or south.
5. Elevation in excellence or in rank; utmost degree; as the height of arrogance.
corruption_summary: Men are still measured by height of stature — presence, bearing, and appearance — in exactly the way 1 Samuel 16:7 forbids, and the standard is applied to the choosing of leaders.
corruption_paragraphs: 1 Samuel 16:7 is quoted often and obeyed rarely, and its setting is what gives it force. Samuel is not a worldly man; he is the prophet who anointed Saul, and Saul's height had been a selling point — from his shoulders and upward he was higher than any of the people, and it had ended badly. Now, standing before Eliab, Samuel makes the same judgment again, and God stops him mid-thought. If a prophet with that experience could be taken in by a man's build, the rest of us should assume we are. The application to choosing elders is direct: 1 Timothy 3 lists character almost exclusively, and a church that selects for bearing and presence is applying a criterion God explicitly refused.

The principle to recover is where height ends up in Romans 8. Paul is piling up everything that might be thought to reach far enough to reach a believer — death, life, angels, principalities, powers, things present, things to come, height, depth, and any other creature — and the point of the list is that it is a list of creatures. Nothing made can undo what the Maker has done. Height, which is the dimension men use to overawe each other and which the tower-builders of Babel reached for, is filed among the things that cannot separate us from the love of God which is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
roots_summary: Hebrew qomah is stature or height; gobah is loftiness, and carries the sense of pride. Greek hupsoma is a high thing or elevation, the word in Romans 8:39.
roots_lines: Hebrew qomah (H6967) — height, stature; the height of the ark and of a man.
Hebrew gobah (H1363) — loftiness, elevation; used of pride and of haughtiness of heart.
Hebrew rum (H7311) — to be high, to be lifted up; the root of both exaltation and arrogance.
Greek hupsoma (G5313) — a high thing, elevation; height in Romans 8:39.
Greek hupsos (G5311) — height, high place; the height named in Ephesians 3:18.

Of a measure God refuses: look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature (1 Samuel 16:7).

pos: a. (before in time; the first of two; belonging to the past; rendering Hebrew rishon, Greek proteros)
etymology: A double comparative from forme, first, on the pattern of latter. Hebrew rishon is from rosh, the head, and means first or foremost — so the former things are the head of the sequence, what came before.
biblical_def: Former points backwards, and Scripture gives careful and sometimes surprising instructions about how to regard what lies there. Isaiah commands a startling forgetfulness: “Remember ye not the former things, neither consider the things of old” (Isaiah 43:18) — and this from the prophet who has just recounted the exodus, so the command is not against remembering as such but against letting the old deliverance become the ceiling of expectation; the next verse says Behold, I will do a new thing. Ecclesiastes forbids nostalgia in blunter terms: “Say not thou, What is the cause that the former days were better than these? for thou dost not enquire wisely concerning this” (Ecclesiastes 7:10). The verdict is not that the past was worse but that the question is unwise — it cannot be answered honestly and it does nothing but corrode the present. Paul uses the word for the discarded self: “put off concerning the former conversation the old man, which is corrupt according to the deceitful lusts” (Ephesians 4:22), where conversation means the whole manner of life. And Revelation gives the last use, at the end of all sorrow: “there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away” (Revelation 21:4).
webster_summary: What came before. Isaiah forbids making the old deliverance the ceiling of hope; Ecclesiastes calls nostalgia unwise enquiry; Paul makes the former manner of life a garment to put off; and in the end the former things pass away.
webster_full: FORMER, a. [a comparative from forme, first.] Before in time; preceding another or something else in order of time.
2. Ancient; long past; as in former ages.
3. Mentioned before another; as, the former and the latter of two things.
4. Past, as opposed to present; as, my former state of life.
5. Former rain, the early rain of autumn, as distinguished from the latter rain of spring, Joel 2.
corruption_summary: The past is either idolised as a golden age — the enquiry Ecclesiastes calls unwise — or discarded entirely, so that a church loses the fathers, the confessions, and the memory of God's dealings.
corruption_paragraphs:
Ecclesiastes 7:10 diagnoses a permanent temptation and does not flatter it. Asking why the former days were better is called unwise enquiry, and the reason is that the question is malformed: it assumes what it asks, it compares a remembered past with an experienced present, and it produces discontent without producing action. This is worth saying carefully, because a confessional Christian is committed to honouring the past — the Reformers, the Puritans, the 1689 — and there is a real difference between honouring fathers and pining for a decade. Isaiah 43:18 draws the same line from the other side: do not let what God did last time set the limit on what you expect him to do next.

The opposite failure is the church that has cut itself loose from everything former, treating the fathers as irrelevant and the confessions as constraints. It always ends by rediscovering old heresies at great cost, because a body with no memory cannot recognise anything.

The principle to recover is Paul's image in Ephesians 4:22, where the former manner of life is a garment. Clothing is not the self; it is worn, and it can be taken off and left off. That is a mercy for anyone whose past is the thing he cannot get out from under. And the final word on the subject is Revelation 21:4, where the former things do not merely stop mattering, they pass away — death, sorrow, crying, and pain named individually and abolished, with God himself wiping the tears. Christians are not asked to pretend the former things were nothing. They are told what will become of them.

Greek proteros (G4387) — former, earlier; the former conversation, Ephesians 4:22.

pos: a. and adv. (single; without company; by itself only; rendering Hebrew bad and levad, Greek monos)
etymology: From all and one — al one, wholly by oneself. The same compound, worn down further, gives lone and lonely. Hebrew levad means in separation, apart.
biblical_def: Alone receives the first negative verdict in Scripture. In a creation repeatedly pronounced good, one thing is not: “It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him” (Genesis 2:18) — spoken before the fall, so human aloneness is a deficiency in the created order rather than a consequence of sin, and the remedy God provides is another person. Ecclesiastes reasons practically to the same conclusion: “if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow: but woe to him that is alone when he falleth; for he hath not another to help him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:10). The word also marks the limits of what will sustain a man. In the wilderness our Lord answers the first temptation: “It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4) — bread is not denied, it is denied the whole office. And the most searching use is his own, hours before the arrest: “the hour cometh, yea, is now come, that ye shall be scattered, every man to his own, and shall leave me alone: and yet I am not alone, because the Father is with me” (John 16:32). He states both facts without softening either. He was left alone by every friend, and he was not alone — until Golgotha, where he asked why he had been forsaken, so that his people never need to.
webster_summary: Single; without company. It is the first thing in creation called not good; Ecclesiastes pities the man who falls alone; bread alone will not sustain a man; and Christ, left alone by all, says the Father is with him.
webster_full: ALONE, a. [all and one.] Single; solitary; without the presence of another; applied to a person or thing.
2. It is applied to a person or thing which is by itself, or which excludes all others; as, God alone is holy.
3. ALONE, adv. Separately; by itself.
4. To let alone, to suffer to rest; to forbear molesting or meddling with.
5. In Scripture, it is not good that the man should be alone, Gen. 2; man shall not live by bread alone, Matt. 4.
corruption_summary: Isolation is chosen and called independence, against the first not good in Scripture — while the solas, which use the word rightly, are softened by adding something to faith, grace, Christ, Scripture, or God's glory.
corruption_paragraphs:
Genesis 2:18 is a pre-fall verdict, and it settles a good deal. Man's need of others is not a weakness introduced by sin but a feature of how God made him, and the arrangements Scripture gives for it are marriage, family, and the local church — embodied, committed, and inconvenient. An age that can simulate company at any hour has made isolation comfortable enough to choose, and calls it independence. Ecclesiastes answers with a scene rather than an argument: a man falls, and there is nobody to lift him up. That is not a description of loneliness as an emotion but of a practical exposure, and it is why Hebrews commands the assembling of ourselves together and warns against the manner of some who forsake it.

There is a right use of the word, and it is the Reformation's. Grace alone, faith alone, Christ alone, Scripture alone, to the glory of God alone — and in every case the word does its work by excluding. Add anything to any of the five and the doctrine is gone: faith plus merit is not faith alone, and Scripture plus tradition as a coordinate authority is not Scripture alone.

The principle to recover is John 16:32, which holds two things together that a believer must learn to hold. Christ says plainly that his friends will scatter and leave him alone, and in the same breath that he is not alone, because the Father is with him. Both are true, and the second does not cancel the sting of the first. That is the pattern for every Christian abandoned by those who should have stood by him. And there is one point at which the pattern does not transfer: on the cross he was forsaken by the Father too, and the cry of dereliction was uttered so that Hebrews could promise the rest of us I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
